client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago. Every time I go to a family gathering, it just hits me all over again — like this wave of sadness I can't control, and I end up feeling worse than if I'd just stayed home. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: It means a lot that you decided to reach out, even with that uncertainty — that takes real courage. Losing your dad and then having those waves of grief hit you at family gatherings, in places that probably hold so many memories of him, sounds genuinely painful and exhausting. I'm curious — when you imagine staying home to avoid those gatherings, what does that feel like in your mind: more like relief, or more like something else?

client: Honestly, when I think about staying home, it feels like relief at first — like I can just breathe without worrying about breaking down in front of everyone. But then pretty quickly it turns into this guilty, hollow feeling, like I'm somehow letting my dad down or abandoning the rest of the family. So it's not really relief, it's more like I'm just trading one bad feeling for a different one.
therapist: What you just described shows a lot of self-awareness — you're caught between two painful options, and neither one feels like a true escape, just a different kind of hurt. That guilt about "letting your dad down" is worth gently exploring, because it sounds like a very powerful thought that's shaping how you feel in both directions. Where do you think that belief comes from — is it something you feel your dad would have actually wanted for you, or more like a rule you've placed on yourself?

client: That's a hard question, because honestly, my dad was the kind of person who always wanted the family together — Sunday dinners, holidays, all of it. So part of me thinks he would have wanted me there, but then another part of me wonders if I'm just using what I think he would have wanted to beat myself up, if that makes sense. I'm not sure I can easily separate what was really "him" from what's just become this voice in my head that judges everything I do.
therapist: That insight — recognizing that the voice judging you might not actually *be* your dad, but something you've constructed in grief — is really profound and takes a lot of honesty to see. It makes sense that after losing someone so central to your life, their values and wishes would become internalized, but grief can sometimes twist that into something harsher than the person ever actually was. If the dad who loved bringing family together could see you right now, struggling and doing your best, what do you think he'd actually say to you?

client: I want to say he'd tell me it's okay, that he'd understand — and when I really sit with it, I think maybe he would. But it's hard to hold onto that thought because it almost feels like if I let myself off the hook, I'm somehow accepting that he's gone, and I'm not ready for that. So even when I try to imagine him being kind to me, it kind of breaks down into this fresh wave of grief all over again.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really important — the self-criticism might actually be serving a purpose, keeping you connected to him in a way, because softening it feels like taking a step toward accepting a loss you're not ready for yet. That's not a flaw in you; that's grief doing what grief does, trying to protect you from pain even while causing a different kind of pain. I'm wondering — does it feel possible that you could hold both things at once, letting him be kind to you *and* still not being ready to fully let go?

client: I hear what you're saying, and it's an interesting idea, but I'm not sure I actually know how to do that — hold two contradictory things at the same time without one of them canceling the other out. It feels like my brain just doesn't work that way, like it wants to pick a side and stick with it. I guess I'm skeptical that it's something I could just decide to do, even if it makes sense in theory.
therapist: Your skepticism makes complete sense, and I want to be clear — this isn't something you just *decide* to do, it's more like a skill that develops gradually, often in small, almost accidental moments. That all-or-nothing pull you're describing, where your mind wants to pick a side, is actually a really common pattern in grief and something we could gently work with over time rather than overcome all at once. I'm curious — have there ever been other areas of your life, even small ones, where you've managed to hold two conflicting feelings without one completely erasing the other?

client: I had to actually think about that for a minute, and maybe... when my dad was sick, I was terrified of losing him but also genuinely grateful for the extra time we had together. I didn't think of it that way at the time, but I guess both of those things were true at once without one wiping out the other. I'm not sure that's quite the same thing, but it's the closest example I can come up with.
therapist: That example is *exactly* the same thing — you just proved to yourself that your brain actually can hold two painful, contradictory truths at once, even when it doesn't feel that way in the moment. The fact that you found that without me suggesting it tells me that capacity is already inside you, not something you'd have to build from scratch. I wonder if it might be worth gently revisiting that memory sometimes when the all-or-nothing feeling takes over — not as a solution, but just as a reminder that you've already done this before — what do you think?

client: I can see why that makes sense logically, and I guess it's kind of reassuring to realize I've already done it without knowing. But I worry that when I'm actually in the middle of a grief wave — like at a family dinner with his empty chair right there — I won't have the presence of mind to go back to that memory, it'll just feel too far away. It's one thing to connect the dots here in a calm conversation, and another thing entirely when the emotion is hitting me full force.
therapist: You're absolutely right, and it would be unfair to suggest that a calm insight automatically translates into the middle of an emotional storm — that gap between knowing something and being able to use it under pressure is real and worth taking seriously. What might actually help is doing some small, low-stakes practice *before* you're in those intense moments, almost like building a little mental muscle memory so the thought is easier to reach when the wave hits. I'm wondering — in the lead-up to the next family gathering, would you be open to trying something small, like just spending a few quiet minutes with that memory of holding fear and gratitude at the same time, so it feels a little less far away when you need it?

client: I guess I could try that, though I'm a little worried that deliberately sitting with that memory might just open up the grief rather than make me feel more prepared. Like, what if I spend those few minutes before a gathering thinking about when he was sick, and then I show up already emotional instead of more grounded? I don't want to accidentally make things harder for myself right before I walk in the door.
therapist: That's a really thoughtful and practical concern, and it's worth taking seriously rather than just pushing through with the original idea. Maybe the timing and framing matters here — rather than right before a gathering, you might try sitting with that memory at a quieter, safer moment during the week, somewhere you *can* let emotion come without it mattering, so it gradually becomes more familiar and less overwhelming over time. What would feel like a safe enough moment in your week to experiment with that, where if grief did surface, you'd have the space to let it?

client: Maybe Sunday mornings could work — my dad and I used to talk on the phone then, so it's already a time that feels heavy and kind of set apart from the rest of the week. I think I could sit with that memory then without it derailing my whole day, since I'm usually alone and not rushing anywhere. I'm still not entirely sure it'll help, but I suppose it's worth trying once and seeing what happens rather than just assuming it won't work.
therapist: Sunday mornings feel like a really meaningful choice — that time is already holding grief for you, so you'd be working *with* something that's already there rather than introducing something new. And I love the way you framed it: trying once to see what happens rather than assuming it won't work — that's exactly the kind of open, gentle curiosity that makes these small experiments useful. After you try it, I'd be really interested to hear what you notice — not whether it "worked" in some big way, but just what it felt like to sit with that memory in a space you chose for yourself.

client: I appreciate that you're not framing it as something that has to "work" in some big way, because that takes some of the pressure off. I think what I'm most nervous about is that sitting with it intentionally might feel forced or artificial, like I'm performing grief rather than actually feeling it, if that makes any sense. But I guess I won't really know until I try, and at least Sunday mornings already feel like his time in some way.
therapist: That fear of "performing" grief rather than genuinely feeling it is really worth naming, because it shows how much authenticity matters to you — and to your relationship with your dad. The thing is, choosing to show up for a feeling isn't the same as faking it; you already show up for that heaviness on Sunday mornings without choosing it, so intentionally making space for it might feel more natural than you're expecting. What do you think it would feel like if it did turn out to feel genuine rather than forced — would that change anything for you?
